Succession therefore follows the default rule, under which the sister is preferred to the collaterals for non-ancestral property, and the High Court's decision in her favour is upheld.
nn_pred: The burden lies on the party asserting the custom (the collateral) to prove that it displaces personal law, and Riwaj-i-am entries that concern ancestral property do not prove a custom excluding a sister from non-ancestral property. Because the custom was not established, succession is governed by personal law, under which the sister takes in preference to the collaterals.

actual: The explanation to Order IX Rule 13 barred the application to set aside the ex parte decree, even though the application was filed before the appeal and the appeal was dismissed for default rather than decided on its merits.

The Explanation to Order IX Rule 13 therefore applies, and the decree merges with the appellate order. Because the defendant never withdrew the appeal, the pending application did not save the setting-aside remedy.
nn_pred: The application under Order IX Rule 13 would not be maintainable. The appeal was disposed of for default rather than withdrawn, so the Explanation to Order IX Rule 13 bars the setting-aside remedy. The earlier decision's res judicata and issue estoppel reasoning concerns the opposite sequence, an appeal after final setting-aside proceedings, so it does not directly govern. Its principle of finality across successive stages points the same way.

actual: The direction requiring the authority to take action was beyond the High Court’s jurisdiction and was set aside; a court may displace the authority’s decision-making role only in exceptional circumstances supported by cogent reasons.
rule_pred: Yes, the action is invalid. The agreement vested discretion in the authority, to be exercised after notice and a hearing, and the High Court, an external body with no power under the agreement or statute to decide or direct the individual outcome, ordered action against the allottees and left nothing to the authority's discretion. That displaces the authority's own judgment, and the direction should be set aside, with the matter remanded for the authority to decide independently after notice and a hearing.
nn_pred: Yes. A decision is invalid where a statutory authority, in substance, acts under the dictation of a superior or external body with no statutory power over the matter, because the authority has surrendered its own discretion. Here the High Court directed the authority to take action against the allottees, removing the discretion the agreement gave it (after notice and hearing), and gave no reason why the authority could not decide independently. So the direction cannot stand, and the matter should go back to the authority to exercise its own discretion.

actual: The Court was not satisfied that the property had been sold at a low price and rejected this ground for invalidating the sale.
rule_pred: No. The Supreme Court would likely hold that the sale cannot be set aside merely because the price was allegedly inadequate. The appellant did not prove that the property was worth more than its own earlier valuation, and the trial court found no fraud. Without proof of fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale that caused substantial injury (Order XXI Rule 90 CPC), price inadequacy alone is not a ground for setting aside the sale.
nn_pred: No. The sale cannot be set aside merely because the price was allegedly inadequate. The challenger must prove fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale (Order XXI Rule 90 CPC) and resulting substantial injury, and here the trial court found no fraud and the evidence did not show the property was worth more than the appellant's own earlier valuation, so the challenge fails.

actual: The transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale, not an absolute sale with a right of repurchase, and the transferors could redeem the properties. The appeal was dismissed.
rule_pred: The court will most likely classify the transaction as a mortgage by conditional sale, so the transferors can redeem, and not as an outright sale with a right of repurchase. The decisive reasons are that the deed is read as a whole with the surrounding circumstances. The consideration went to discharge existing debts. The transferees could force the transferors to take the properties back and repay the consideration, which shows a personal liability for repayment. The same-day agreement made the transferors pay the difference between net rents and interest, which looks like interest on a loan. The prices were well below the properties' value. The reconveyance condition is in the same deed, not a separate document.
nn_pred: The Court will most likely hold the transaction to be a mortgage (by conditional sale) and not an outright sale with a right of repurchase, so the transferors' suit for redemption succeeds. The deed and the same-day agreement together show a debtor-creditor relationship and a transfer made as security: the consideration was used to clear the transferors' debts, the transferees could force a reconveyance and repayment of the price, the transferors had to pay the difference between net rents and interest until reconveyance, and the properties were worth far more than the stated prices.

actual: The occupants did not acquire deemed-tenant status and remained licensees, not statutory tenants.

The eleven-month licence was not renewed and so expired before that date, and continued occupation after expiry does not make the occupant a licensee. The other occupant produced no licence agreement showing a subsisting licence on that date, so the claim fails on the evidence.
nn_pred: The Court would hold that neither occupant is a deemed tenant. Under Sections 5(4A), 5(11)(bb) and 15A of the Bombay Rents Act, protection requires occupation under a subsisting licence on the statutory date. One occupant's eleven-month licence was not renewed and so had expired before that date, and the other produced no licence showing a subsisting agreement on that date, so neither can rely on the Act to bar the cooperative proceeding.

actual: The later suit was barred by res judicata against the two defendants for whom the adverse-possession finding had become final, but not against the other defendants.
rule_pred: The Supreme Court would likely hold that the adverse-possession/title finding in the earlier rent-and-possession suit bars the plaintiff from relitigating title in the later suit, at least as against the two defendants whose appeal was dismissed as time-barred. The same parties and property were involved, title and the alleged tenancy were directly and substantially in issue and were actually decided against the plaintiff, the finding was necessary to refuse rent and possession, and it became final as to those defendants because it was not disturbed in the later appeals. The renewed reliance on the same tenancy therefore operates as res judicata.
nn_pred: The earlier finding that the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession, and the rejection of the alleged tenancy, was a final determination on a matter directly and substantially in issue between the same parties, and it was not disturbed in the later appeals. The plaintiff is therefore barred by res judicata (Section 11 CPC, including Explanation IV) from relitigating title or the tenancy claim in the later suit, and the dismissal of the appeal as time-barred against two defendants left the finding final as to them.

actual: The transferees of the earlier mortgagee’s interest were entitled to possession of the property.
rule_pred: Yes. The earlier mortgagee's completed purchase in execution means he acquired the mortgagor's equity of redemption, so the mortgagor's right of redemption is extinguished as against him, and the redemption claims of the later mortgagees (and of persons claiming through them) are subordinated. As the prior mortgagee, he holds the superior right to redeem the later mortgages, and his transferees take that position, so their claim to possession against those occupying under him succeeds.
nn_pred: Yes. The earlier mortgagee's purchase in execution was an act of the parties/court process that extinguished the mortgagor's right of redemption as against that purchaser, merging the equity of redemption with the mortgagee's interest. Redemption claims against the purchaser and his transferees therefore fail or are subordinated, and the purchaser holds a preferential right to redeem the later mortgages.

actual: The late applications were barred, and compensation granted on their basis was illegal; the challenged orders granting that compensation were set aside.
rule_pred: No. The applications were filed after the three-month period under section 28A, so they fall outside the statutory redetermination remedy. They also seek more than a clerical or arithmetical correction. The final awards therefore cannot be reopened, and the Collector's orders granting enhanced compensation are without jurisdiction and void.
nn_pred: No. A final award or decree cannot be reopened through a fresh application or redetermination to obtain additional compensation or benefits the Act does not allow in that proceeding. Once the award is final, relief is limited to the statutory correction power (section 13-A of the Act and section 152 CPC), and inherent power under section 151 CPC cannot create jurisdiction where the Act defines the authority's powers. The Collector therefore lacked jurisdiction to enhance compensation on the time-barred redetermination applications, and those orders are void and liable to be set aside.

The application form and notice expressly disclaimed any obligation to allot, the draw was provisional, the change in land use had not been approved, and no official allotment communication was issued, so the applicants cannot compel allotment or transfer.

actual: The non-examination of the additional persons did not undermine the prosecution case.
rule_pred: The Supreme Court will most likely hold that non-examination of the FIR-named witnesses does not undermine the prosecution case or justify an adverse inference. Section 134 of the Evidence Act sets no minimum number of witnesses, and the prosecution need only call those essential to unfold its case. The appellant did not show that any material witness was deliberately withheld or that the non-examination of the other named witnesses made the prosecution case less trustworthy.

Without a clear order or an express undertaking given to and accepted by the court, there is at most a breach of a consent order between the parties, or a non-compliance that is not shown to be wilful, and that is not enough for contempt.

The earlier principle (wilful breach of an accepted undertaking is contempt, requiring purging as well as a sanction) is therefore not triggered, and the aggrieved party must pursue ordinary remedies such as execution.

So no tenant protection and no registration requirement as a lease follow.

He therefore gets no tenant protection, and no registration-as-lease question arises. The decisive reasons are the signed writing disclaiming tenancy, the supporting testimony, the free use of hospital facilities and staff, and receipts that never identify the payments as rent.

actual: The first judgment could be challenged in the appeal from the final judgment; because it was legally erroneous, the subsequent proceedings founded on it were non est.
rule_pred: Yes. The remand order did not terminate the proceedings, and nothing in the guidance indicates a statutory bar (such as CPC Section 105(2)) applies on these facts. The party can therefore challenge the remand order in its appeal from the final High Court judgment, even though it did not appeal the remand order when it was made.
nn_pred: Yes. Because the High Court's first judgment only remanded the case and did not finally terminate the proceedings, the party's failure to appeal it at that stage does not bar a challenge in the appeal from the later final decision. Section 105 CPC permits objections to interlocutory orders affecting the decision, and the res judicata principle of section 11 does not preclude this, as the remand order was non-terminating (unlike the cases where an earlier decision effectively ended the proceedings), subject to the section 105(2) restriction for appealable remand orders, which did not bar the challenge here.

actual: The authorization was merely evidential and did not require registration.
rule_pred: The authorization does not need registration. It was not the operative instrument embodying the bargain: it did not state the principal, the interest rate, or the deeds, and it created no interest in the property. It merely authorized the deposit, so it is admissible to prove the mortgage by deposit of title deeds, which arises from the debt, the delivery of the deeds and the intention to secure the debt.

Because it was not intended to embody the mortgage bargain (it omitted the principal, interest rate, and deed details, and created no interest in the property), the mortgage arose by implication from the deposit of title deeds made with the intention to secure the debt, and the document was merely evidential.

nn_pred: No. The highest bidder acquires no vested right and there is no concluded contract until the competent authority (here the Chief Commissioner) accepts or confirms the bid as the auction terms or rules require; the bid is only an offer. Because the bid was never confirmed and the deposit was not paid, no contract arose, so the Collector cannot recover the difference on resale from the original bidder. The earlier caveat emptor and defect-of-title decision does not govern this question.

Because the allegations of forgery and fabricated documents, taken at face value, prima facie disclosed offences, the High Court had to examine them (per Bhajan Lal) rather than treat the matter as purely civil, and their truth was for trial. actual: The Court could not examine whether the prescribed valuation principles were relevant or whether the compensation was illusory, because the provisions were protected from the asserted property-rights challenge.
rule_pred: The Supreme Court will most likely reject the challenge and uphold the provisions. The law is in the Ninth Schedule, so Article 31-B shields it from a compensation-based attack under the former property guarantee. Even apart from that, a formula tied to an earlier valuation benchmark plus an addition fixes a real, positive amount, which is not illusory merely because it is lower than market value, and inadequacy is not justiciable.
nn_pred: The challenge would fail: because the impugned provisions are part of a law placed in the Ninth Schedule (Article 31-B, along with the protections in Articles 31(4) and 31-A where applicable), the Court cannot inquire into the adequacy of compensation or invalidate the provisions for inconsistency with the property guarantee. A formula limiting market value to an earlier benchmark plus an addition still yields a positive amount, so it is at most inadequate rather than illusory, and the appeals should be dismissed.

nn_pred: The Court will likely hold that Section 357 CrPC lets it order compensation in addition to (or in lieu of further) imprisonment, so it can treat the time already served (about eight years for the three principal attackers, eight months for the grievous hurt accused) as the sentence and direct each appellant to pay compensation to the deceased's widow and children or the injured victim. The amount should reflect the nature of the crime, the injury suffered, the justness of the claim, the accused's capacity to pay and other circumstances, and the original sentence may revive if compensation is not paid.
